job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Drafting review: S. 2817, Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act (as amended Oct. 6, 2026)**

I worked only from the text you pasted. Please check it against the official bill text and amendment on congress.gov, and confirm any statutory references with Committee staff before we publish.

1. **§2(1)(A):** The 10,000-ton threshold applies "by a single vessel," so an operator running several vessels that each stay under the limit falls outside the definition. The test should be applied to the operator or project as a whole.

2. **§2(1)(A):** "Recovery," "mineral resources," "seabed," and "per year" are undefined. It is unclear whether tonnage is wet or dry weight, whether discarded sediment counts, and whether material lifted and returned to the seabed counts as "recovery."

3. **§2(1)(A):** The definition covers only depths "greater than 200 meters." Shallower continental-shelf mining is outside the bill, which may be intended but should be confirmed given the "deep seabed" title.

4. **§2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" is never identified. Section 4 uses NOAA and Section 6 uses State, so the administering agency is unclear.

5. **§2(1)(B):** The catch-all for activities "comparable" in risk gives no criteria, process, notice, or standard of review. That invites disputes over whether a given activity qualifies and challenges to the determination under the Administrative Procedure Act.

6. **§2(2):** The "U.S. person" definition covers citizens and state-chartered corporations only. LLCs, partnerships, and other unincorporated U.S. entities are not included, which weakens the extraterritorial reach in §3(a). "State" is also undefined (D.C. and territories are unclear).

7. **§2(3):** "Equipped for the recovery" is undefined, and so is "vessel." Operators could use several smaller vessels, towed collectors, barges, or support platforms, or remove equipment, to stay below the 5,000-GT threshold that triggers §4.

8. **§§2(1), 2(3), 4:** The bill uses three different terms for the same activity: "polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources," "seabed mineral resources," and "recovery activities." These should be harmonized.

9. **§3(a):** "Engage in" is undefined. It is unclear whether financing, chartering, supplying equipment, or contracting for mining is prohibited.

10. **§3(a):** The bill does not prohibit importing, selling, or processing minerals recovered abroad. Output from mining in other jurisdictions could still enter U.S. markets.

11. **§3(a):** "United States" is undefined, so it is unclear whether the prohibition reaches the EEZ, the continental shelf, or U.S.-flagged vessels on the high seas. "Person" is also undefined, which matters for penalties.

12. **§3(b):** The grandfather clause covers any "exploration license" without defining the term, naming the issuing authority, requiring that the license remain valid, or limiting its scope. A license issued for exploration could be used to conduct commercial-scale recovery.

13. **§3(b):** The heading says "existing operations," but the text covers only licenses. Operations under other authorizations are not addressed.

14. **§3(b):** Licenses issued between now and enactment would qualify, and the bill has no anti-evasion or cutoff rule. Issuing licenses before the bill passes is a foreseeable risk.

15. **§3(b) (general):** The bill does not say how it relates to existing law, such as the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980, under which NOAA issues licenses and permits. Staff should confirm whether §3(b) is meant to cover licenses under that act and whether the bill amends or overrides it.

16. **§3(c):** The environmental-assessment exception has no limits on quantity, duration, or sale of recovered material, and it requires no notice or certification. A commercial operation could sell large volumes while claiming an assessment purpose, which would be hard to prove or disprove.

17. **§4(a):** Registration has no deadline, no content requirements, and no penalty for failure. The bill also does not say whether registration confers any authority.

18. **§4(a):** Registration obligations attach only to "covered vessels," but nothing requires anyone to determine which vessels are covered. An operator who does not register is never identified as covered.

19. **§4(b):** The quarterly report has no required content (tonnage, location, depth), no deadline, no public-availability requirement, and no verification mechanism. It is "certified," but the bill does not say what happens if the certification is false.

20. **§§4–5:** Section 5 penalizes only violations of §3. Failing to register, failing to report, or filing a false report carries no penalty.

21. **§5(a) vs. §8:** Section 5(a) applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §8 makes the whole Act, including §3, effective 180 days after enactment. The two provisions conflict on whether conduct in the 180-day window is penalized.

22. **§5(a):** "For each day" is unclear. It is not stated whether a day means each day of operation, each vessel, or each ton recovered. The subsection also names no enforcing agency, no assessment procedure, no injunction authority, no statute of limitations, and no forfeiture of vessels or equipment.

23. **§5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined. The subsection does not address officers and directors, attempts, conspiracy, or whether penalties apply per count or per day.

24. **§5 (general):** The bill has no citizen-suit or private right of action provision, so enforcement depends entirely on agency action. This may be a policy choice, but it should be flagged for discussion.

25. **§6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates an obligation to try, not to succeed. The bill has no reporting requirement, no consequence if no agreement is reached, and no definition of "equivalent" prohibitions. It also does not address the International Seabed Authority or how U.S. rules would interact with its processes, and the United States is not a party to UNCLOS.

26. **§7(a) vs. §7(b):** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect until a joint resolution is enacted, but §7(b) says the entire Act ceases to have effect after 10 years. Staff need to determine whether the ban ends at year 10 regardless of any finding.

27. **§7(a):** "Serious harm" is undefined, and it is unclear whether the standard applies to a single project or the industry. The NASEM report has no deadline, and the bill does not require Congress to act within any period after receiving it.

28. **§7(a):** A joint resolution must be presented to the President and is subject to veto. That affects how the lifting mechanism works in practice, and the bill does not explain how it would operate.

29. **§7(b):** The sunset runs from enactment, not from the §8 effective date, so the Act is in force for about 9.5 years rather than 10. The bill also has no savings clause, leaving liability for violations during the effective period, and pending enforcement actions, unclear after sunset.

30. **§8:** The bill has no transition rules for operations already underway or licenses in process. Combined with §3(b)'s reference to the enactment date, the 180-day window could allow licenses to be issued and operations expanded before the prohibition takes effect.

31. **General:** The bill has no severability clause, no rulemaking authority, no definitions section, and no appropriation for enforcement. Without rulemaking authority, implementation would rely on guidance, which is easier to challenge.

**Suggested priorities for Thursday's markup:**
- Resolve the §7(a)/§7(b) conflict and the sunset start date (items 26, 29).
- Fix the penalty-date conflict between §5(a) and §8 (item 21).
- Close the grandfather loophole in §3(b) and the assessment exception in §3(c) (items 12–14, 16).
- Address per-vessel and per-operator thresholds, and the "covered vessel" definition (items 1, 7).
- Name the administering agency and add rulemaking authority, enforcement mechanisms, and penalties for §4 violations (items 4, 20, 22, 31).

If useful, I can turn the priority items into questions for committee staff or a short explainer section.
